cards.explanation: The answer is that they serve the Baals and the Asherahs. The text says they "…forgot the LORD their God and served the Baals and the Asherahs." (Judges 3:7) Those are false gods. Notice the forgetting doesn't leave an empty spot, because something else steps right in.

The answer is that they serve him for eight years. The LORD sells Israel into the hand of Cushan-rishathaim, and the text says "…the Israelites served him eight years." (Judges 3:8) So they're serving a king who isn't theirs, and this verse doesn't mention a quick way out. Eight years is a long time to wait on one timer.

The answer is True. The text says, "…when the Israelites cried out to the LORD, He raised up Othniel…" (Judges 3:9) After eight years of serving a foreign king, they call out. And the LORD answers by raising up a deliverer. Don't ever let anyone tell you crying out is a waste of breath.

The word is "prevails." The LORD delivers Cushan-rishathaim into Othniel's hand, and Othniel "…prevailed against him." (Judges 3:10) Othniel is Caleb's nephew, the son of Caleb's younger brother Kenaz (Judges 3:9). The Spirit of the LORD came upon him first, and then he went out to war.

The answer is False. The text says "…the land had rest for forty years, until Othniel son of Kenaz died." (Judges 3:11) So the rest doesn't end until Othniel dies. Forty years, friends, that's a long quiet.

The answer is that He gives a foreign king power over Israel. The text says, "…He gave Eglon king of Moab power over Israel, because they had done evil in the sight of the LORD." (Judges 3:12) Eglon is the king of Moab, a nation east of Israel. That's the second time in this passage a foreign king gets power over them.

The answer is eighteen. "The Israelites served Eglon king of Moab eighteen years." (Judges 3:14) Earlier they served Cushan-rishathaim eight years (Judges 3:8). Eighteen is more than double that, and that's a long time to wait on a timer.

The answer is True. The text says, "So they sent him with tribute to Eglon king of Moab." (Judges 3:15) Tribute is the payment a conquered people brings to the king over them. So Ehud walks right up to Eglon with a reason to be there.

The answer is his right thigh. The text says Ehud "…strapped it to his right thigh under his cloak" (Judges 3:16) For a left-handed man, I think that's a smart spot, since his left hand reaches across for it. Later the text says he pulls it from that right thigh (Judges 3:21).

The answer is "I have a secret message for you." Ehud says, "I have a secret message for you, O king." (Judges 3:19) A secret message is a good reason to clear a room. He's turned back from the idols near Gilgal to say it. And the king takes him seriously.

The answer is False. Ehud says, "I have a word from God for you…" and the text says "…the king rose from his seat." (Judges 3:20) So Eglon stands up. This is a heavy part of the story, and I think it's best to take it in slowly.

The word is "locking." The text says Ehud went out "…closing and locking the doors of the upper room behind him." (Judges 3:23) That's why the servants run into locked doors in the next verse. It's a small detail that matters a lot.

The answer is that he's relieving himself in the cool room. The servants say, "He must be relieving himself in the cool room…" (Judges 3:24) They find locked doors and come up with the most ordinary guess they can. I think nobody wants to be the one who knocks on that door, and that's the whole story of the waiting.

The word is "key." The text says, "Then they took the key and opened the doors…" (Judges 3:25) They wait until they're worried, and then they use the key. What they find is their lord lying dead on the floor. That's a sober moment, friends.

The answer is True. The text says, "Ehud, however, had escaped while the servants waited." (Judges 3:26) He passes by the idols and gets away to Seirah. All that waiting outside the doors gave him a head start.

The answer is that he blows the ram's horn. The text says, "…he blew the ram’s horn throughout the hill country of Ephraim." (Judges 3:27) A ram's horn is a loud call that carries across hills. And the Israelites come down with him.

The answer is True. Ehud tells them, "Follow me, for the LORD has delivered your enemies the Moabites into your hand." (Judges 3:28) He doesn't say he did this himself. He points to the LORD, and the people follow him down.

The answer is that they let no one cross over. The text says they seized the fords of the Jordan leading to Moab, "…and they did not allow anyone to cross over." (Judges 3:28) A ford is a shallow spot where people can cross a river. Hold the crossings and nobody gets through.
The answer is eighty. The text says, "…the land had rest for eighty years." (Judges 3:30) Compare that to the forty years of rest after Othniel (Judges 3:11). Eighty is double, friends.

The answer is an oxgoad. The text says Shamgar "…saved Israel, striking down six hundred Philistines with an oxgoad." (Judges 3:31) An oxgoad is a long pointed stick for driving oxen, so it's a farm tool. I can't even win a fight with a rolling pin, friends.
